panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Clinical photograph of typical groin lesions explicitly described as small abscesses without scarring or sinus tracts, consistent with Hurley stage I hidradenitis suppurativa. B: Clinical photograph showing recurrent axillary abscesses, initial sinus tracts, and scarring, explicitly classified as Hurley stage II hidradenitis suppurativa. C: Clinical photograph showing diffuse axillary disease with large abscesses, interconnected sinus tracts, and scarring, explicitly classified as Hurley stage III hidradenitis suppurativa.

in_text_mentions: HS is usually localized in the apocrine gland-bearing areas (Figure 1). According to the modified Dessau definition, three diagnostic criteria should be matched: presence of typical lesions, typical locations, and chronicity [10]. Deep-seated painful nodules, abscesses, suppurative sinus tracts or tunnels, bridged scars, and double- and multi-ended comedones (also known as “tombstone comedones”) are described as typical lesions. panels.rationale: The image is a labeled H&E punch-biopsy section from the gluteal region, and the caption explicitly describes characteristic histologic features of hidradenitis suppurativa, including follicular occlusion, suppurative inflammation, fibrosis, and an epithelialized sinus tract.

panels.figure_caption: Typical histological features of HS. Sample acquired by punch biopsy from gluteal region. Hyperparakeratosis and papillomatosis (1), follicular hyperkeratosis and perifolliculitis (2), fibrosis (3), abscess-like accumulation of neutrophils and spotted infiltrate of lymphocytes/plasma cells (4), epithelialized sinus tract with surrounding inflammatory reaction (5).
in_text_mentions: ted perifolliculitis [4]. In this scenario, bacterial colonization is considered a secondary pathogenic factor that can worsen HS [2,4]. Indeed, HS lesions formation starts with follicular occlusion which leads to dilatation followed by rupture, resulting in extrusion of the follicular contents, including keratin and bacteria, into the surrounding dermis with the induction of an intense inflammatory response from neutrophils and lymphocytes (Figure 2). The perifollicular inflammatory cellular infiltrate causes abscess formation, leading to the destruction of the pilosebaceous unit [2,4,63,64].
